after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Three linked cards show supply-chain disruption as a global question about risk, a national question about making essential goods at home, and a local shop that cannot restock. Below, glocalisation, popularised by Roland Robertson in the 1990s, describes global products adapted to local cultures, with a strength and a limitation.
caption: The same globalisation issue looks different from the world, a country and one shop.

after: ## Different perspectives and why people hold them
alt: Three columns of perspectives on globalisation: supportive (cheaper goods, new jobs, spread of ideas), middle ground (managed trade through fair trade and labour standards) and critical (job losses, wage pressure, transport emissions, cultural loss). Friedman’s The World Is Flat (2005) and Stiglitz’s Globalization and Its Discontents (2002) show informed experts disagree.
caption: Informed experts disagree about globalisation, so present each view fairly before judging.

alt: Three causes, container shipping from 1956, the World Trade Organization from 1995 and digital communication, lead to long supply chains across many countries. Two consequences follow: a worldwide computer chip shortage in 2020 and 2021 that cut car production, and the Ever Given blocking the Suez Canal for six days in March 2021.
caption: Cheaper shipping, trade rules and the internet linked the world, but long supply chains can be fragile.

alt: Fifty dots, 31 highlighted, show that 31 of 50 Pellmoor shopkeepers said a global supermarket forced a neighbour to close. The evidence has value as direct experience but is a small sample from one town, from people with a vested interest, reporting beliefs not checked closures; the general conclusion is an unsupported generalisation.
caption: A belief reported by a small, interested group cannot prove a general claim.

alt: Tariffs on imports branch into three effects: some factory jobs protected in the short term as imports become dearer; consumers, including protected workers, paying higher prices; and other countries replying with tariffs that cost exporting jobs. The judgement: tariffs may move the problem unless temporary and linked to retraining.
caption: Follow an action to everyone it affects before judging it.

alt: A table of five actions with a benefit and drawback each: fair trade labelling, the 2021 OECD agreement on a 15% global minimum tax, tariffs, buy-local campaigns and spreading suppliers across countries. Below, four things to judge any action by: likely effect, who carries it out, cost and side effects.
caption: Every action on globalisation has someone who pays for it.
